1→use bls12_381::{traits::*, Scalar};
     2→use polynomial::domain::Domain;
     3→
     4→/// Reverses the least significant `bits` of the given number `n`.
     5→///
     6→/// `n` - The input number whose bits are to be reversed.
     7→/// `bits` - The number of least significant bits to reverse.
     8→///
     9→/// Returns a new `usize` with the specified number of bits reversed.
    10→///
    11→/// Taken and modified from: https://github.com/Plonky3/Plonky3/blob/a374139abead1008f84a439e95bb495e81ea4be5/util/src/lib.rs#L67-L76
    12→pub(crate) const fn reverse_bits(n: usize, bits: u32) -> usize {
    13→    // NB: The only reason we need overflowing_shr() here as opposed
    14→    // to plain '>>' is to accommodate the case n == num_bits == 0,
    15→    // which would become `0 >> 64`. Rust thinks that any shift of 64
    16→    // bits causes overflow, even when the argument is zero.
    17→    n.reverse_bits().overflowing_shr(usize::BITS - bits).0
    18→}
    19→
    20→/// Computes log2 of an integer.
    21→///
    22→/// Panics if the integer is not a power of two
    23→pub(crate) const fn log2(x: u32) -> u32 {
    24→    assert!(x > 0 && x.is_power_of_two(), "x must be a power of two.");
    25→    x.trailing_zeros()
    26→}
    27→
    28→/// In-place bit-reversal permutation of a slice.
    29→///
    30→/// Reorders the elements of the slice `a` in-place by reversing the binary representation of their indices.
    31→///
    32→/// For example, if `a.len() == 8` (i.e., `log2(n) = 3`), the index permutation would be:
    33→///
    34→/// ```text
    35→/// Index  Binary   Reversed   Swapped With
    36→/// -----  -------  ---------  -------------
    37→///   0     000       000           -
    38→///   1     001       100           4
    39→///   2     010       010           -
    40→///   3     011       110           6
    41→///   4     100       001           1
    42→///   5     101       101           -
    43→///   6     110       011           3
    44→///   7     111       111           -
    45→/// ```
    46→///
    47→/// This transformation is its own inverse, so applying it twice restores the original order.
    48→///
    49→/// # Panics
    50→/// Panics if the slice length is not a power of two.
    51→///
    52→/// # Arguments
    53→/// * `a` — A mutable slice of data to reorder in-place.
    54→///
    55→/// Taken and modified from: https://github.com/filecoin-project/ec-gpu/blob/bdde768d0613ae546524c5612e2ad576a646e036/ec-gpu-gen/src/fft_cpu.rs#L10C8-L10C18
    56→pub fn reverse_bit_order<T>(a: &mut [T]) {
    57→    // If we are looking for optimizations, it would be nice to have a look at the following:
    58→    // https://github.com/Plonky3/Plonky3/blob/a374139abead1008f84a439e95bb495e81ea4be5/matrix/src/util.rs#L36-L57
    59→
    60→    let n = a.len() as u32;
    61→
    62→    // Ensure the length is a power of two for valid bit-reversal indexing
    63→    assert!(n.is_power_of_two(), "n must be a power of two");
    64→
    65→    // Compute the number of bits needed to index `n` elements (i.e., log2(n))
    66→    let log_n = log2(n);
    67→
    68→    // Iterate through each index and swap with its bit-reversed counterpart
    69→    for k in 0..n {
    70→        // Compute bit-reversed index of k using only log_n bits
    71→        let rk = reverse_bits(k as usize, log_n) as u32;
    72→
    73→        // Swap only if k < rk to avoid double-swapping
    74→        if k < rk {
    75→            a.swap(rk as usize, k as usize);
    76→        }
    77→    }
    78→}
    79→
    80→/// Generate all of the field elements needed to generate the cosets.
    81→///
    82→/// - num_points denotes how many points we want to open the polynomial at.
    83→///   `num_points` can also be seen as the size of the domain.
    84→/// - num_cosets denotes how many cosets we want to generate, analogously how many proofs we want to produce.
    85→///
    86→/// Returns a `Vec<Scalar>` containing the generated coset elements with length `num_cosets`
    87→///
    88→/// Note: Setting bit_reversed to true will generate the cosets in bit-reversed order.
    89→pub fn coset_gens(num_points: usize, num_cosets: usize, bit_reversed: bool) -> Vec<Scalar> {
    90→    // Compute the generator for the group containing all of the points.
    91→    //
    92→    // Note: generating the whole group, just to get the generator is inefficient
    93→    // However, this code is not on the hot path, so we don't optimize it.
    94→    let coset_gen = Domain::new(num_points).generator;
    95→
    96→    // Compute the number of bits needed to represent `num_cosets` indices.
    97→    let bits = log2(num_cosets as u32);
    98→
    99→    // Generate each coset generator as a power of `coset_gen`.
   100→    (0..num_cosets)
   101→        .map(|i| {
   102→            // Optionally bit-reverse the exponent index.
   103→            let exp = if bit_reversed {
   104→                reverse_bits(i, bits)
   105→            } else {
   106→                i
   107→            };
   108→            // Raise the coset generator to the computed exponent.
   109→            coset_gen.pow_vartime([exp as u64])
   110→        })
   111→        .collect()
   112→}
   113→
   114→/// Given a group of coset evaluations, this method will return/reorder the evaluations as if
   115→/// we evaluated them on the relevant extended domain.
   116→///
   117→/// Note: `domain_order` refers to the order that the evaluations would be in, if they were evaluated on
   118→/// the roots of unity. This is different to the order that we return them in; bit-reversed order.
   119→///
   120→/// The coset indices returned can be used to locate the coset_evaluations in the new flattened order:
   121→///   - The idea is that a particular coset evaluation is evenly distributed across the set of flattened
   122→///     evaluations.
   123→///
   124→/// Example:
   125→///   - Let's say we have `k` cosets. Each coset holds `m` values. Each coset will have an associated index.
   126→///   - Once this method has completed, we will be given a flattened set of evaluations where the
   127→///     `m` values in each coset are now a distance of `k` values apart from each other.
   128→///   - The first value that was in the first coset, will be in position `0`.
   129→///   - The second value that was in the first coset, will be in position `k`
   130→///   - The third value that was in the first coset, will be in position `2k`
   131→///   - The first value that was in the second coset, will NOT be in position `1`
   132→///     Instead it will be in position `t = reverse_bit_order(1, k)`.
   133→///   - This value of `t` is what the function returns alongside the flattened evaluations,
   134→///     allowing the caller to deduce the other positions.
   135→///
   136→///
   137→/// Note: For evaluations that are missing, this method will fill these in with zeroes.
   138→///
   139→/// Note: It is the callers responsibility to ensure that there are no duplicate
   140→/// coset indices.
   141→pub fn recover_evaluations_in_domain_order(
   142→    domain_size: usize,
   143→    coset_indices: Vec<usize>,
   144→    coset_evaluations: Vec<Vec<Scalar>>,
   145→) -> Option<(Vec<usize>, Vec<Scalar>)> {
   146→    assert_eq!(coset_indices.len(), coset_evaluations.len());
   147→
   148→    if coset_indices.is_empty() {
   149→        return None;
   150→    }
   151→
   152→    let mut elements = vec![Scalar::ZERO; domain_size];
   153→
   154→    // Check that each coset has the same size
   155→    let coset_len = coset_evaluations[0].len();
   156→    let same_len = coset_evaluations
   157→        .iter()
   158→        .all(|coset| coset.len() == coset_len);
   159→    if !same_len {
   160→        return None;
   161→    }
   162→
   163→    // Check that none of the indices are "out of bounds"
   164→    // This would result in the subsequent indexing operations to panic
   165→    //
   166→    // The greatest index we will be using is:
   167→    // `t = coset_index * coset_len`
   168→    // Let's denote the returned vectors length as `k`
   169→    // We want t < k
   170→    // => coset_index * coset_len < k
   171→    // => coset_index < k / coset_len
   172→    let coset_capacity = domain_size / coset_len;
   173→    if coset_indices.iter().any(|&i| i >= coset_capacity) {
   174→        return None;
   175→    }
   176→
   177→    // Iterate over each coset evaluation set and place the evaluations in the correct locations
   178→    for (&coset_index, coset_evals) in coset_indices.iter().zip(coset_evaluations) {
   179→        let start = coset_index * coset_len;
   180→        elements[start..start + coset_len].copy_from_slice(&coset_evals);
   181→    }
   182→
   183→    // Now bit reverse the result, so we get the evaluations as if we had just done
   184→    // and FFT on them. ie we computed the evaluation set and did not do a reverse bit order.
   185→    reverse_bit_order(&mut elements);
   186→
   187→    // The order of the coset indices in the returned vector will be different.
   188→    // The new indices of the cosets can be figured out by reverse bit ordering
   189→    // the existing indices.
   190→    let num_bits_coset_per_full_domain = log2(coset_capacity as u32);
   191→
   192→    let new_coset_indices = coset_indices
   193→        .into_iter()
   194→        .map(|rbo_coset_index| reverse_bits(rbo_coset_index, num_bits_coset_per_full_domain))
   195→        .collect();
   196→
   197→    Some((new_coset_indices, elements))
   198→}
   199→
   200→/// Generate k = `num_points / points_per_coset` amount of cosets, each containing `points_per_coset` points.
   201→/// The points in each coset will be roots of unity.
   202→/// For FK20, this is a hard requirement for efficient proof generation.
   203→///

   205→/// It will create the same cosets as calling this method with bit_reversed = true
   206→/// However the ordering inside of the cosets will be different.
   207→/// Note: `bit_reverse` on the full group is more concise.
   208→#[cfg(test)]

   210→    num_points: usize,
   211→    points_per_coset: usize,
   212→    bit_reversed: bool,

   215→
   216→    let num_cosets = num_points / points_per_coset;
   217→
   218→    let generators = coset_gens(num_points, num_cosets, bit_reversed);
   219→
   220→    // Manually generate cosets
   221→    let mut cosets = Vec::with_capacity(generators.len());
   222→
   223→    for generator in generators {
   224→        let coset: Vec<Scalar> = subgroup
   225→            .iter()
   226→            .map(|&element| generator * element)
   227→            .collect();
   228→        cosets.push(coset);
   229→    }
   230→
   231→    cosets
   232→}

This depends on **canonical representation**. The `ff::PrimeField` trait specification requires:
